reason: Ten source files use it: seven evaluate model-written programs and workflow scripts in the Node child process, one evaluates model-written plugins inside the host, one compiles a config expression and one is a stub. By the owner's decision there is no embedded interpreter: a model-written program becomes an ordinary script, run as a sandboxed command, that calls tools through the dsh tool command, and every such call goes through the guarded tool pipeline and is logged. Model-written plugins become plugin processes; cross-realm test helpers have no counterpart because Go has one set of types per process.

Worker threads are used for four reasons: keeping slow work off Node's single event loop, bounding memory with a forced stop, isolating third-party code from the ambient environment, and carrying module-loader state. The first maps to goroutines with a context and a bound, the second and third to child processes because a goroutine cannot be killed, and the fourth disappears with the module loader.

Of fifty source files, twenty-one are build scripts, fourteen do plugin and module loading that compiled-in components and plugin processes remove, and four are guest-runtime internals. Three needs survive and use the standard library: finding shipped assets (embed), finding external programs (exec.LookPath) and reading the product version (build information).

Its one use connects the experimental inspector to the host's own V8 debugger. A Go process has no V8 debugger and the DevTools interface is already dropped, so the surviving need, looking inside a running host, is met by Go's profiler and execution tracer behind owner-only loopback endpoints.

Upstream parses model-written programs only to rewrite them around two limits of node:vm (no top-level await in a script, no redeclaration in a retained scope) and to rewrite ES modules for the browser Web Worker runtime; it performs no safety check. By the owner's decision the Go harness has no embedded interpreter: a script is run by whatever interpreter it names, as an ordinary sandboxed command, and the host never parses or rewrites its text, so no JavaScript parser is a dependency.

The tree walker is used by one file, the port of Node's top-level-await transform for vm scripts. That transform is dropped together with the parser because the Go harness evaluates no JavaScript at all and does not rewrite script text.

It exists only because of JavaScript module loading: the experimental Web Worker runtime rewrites ES modules to CommonJS and needs scope analysis to tell an imported name from a local one. A Go program has no modules to rewrite, whether that runtime is dropped or built for WebAssembly.

It is the node-field table that eslint-scope needs to walk a JavaScript syntax tree in the same ES-module-to-CommonJS transform, so it exists only because of JavaScript module loading and has no counterpart in Go.

Upstream parses each config pattern as a Unicode and a non-Unicode JavaScript expression to decide whether the exported JSON Schema may carry it. The exporter and that comparison are dropped by the schema design; the guarantee that an exported pattern means the same to its reader is kept with Go's own regexp parser and a small portable-subset check.

Its only caller prints a source excerpt when a hot-reload compile fails, and hot reload of code is dropped. The idea is kept as one small plain-text function used for rejected config layers and for a malformed argument document given to the dsh tool command (there is no embedded interpreter, so the harness reports no syntax errors in scripts).

Upstream's two-way control pipe between the host and the program child process has no counterpart, because no guest runtime is built. Its job, carrying a script's tool calls to the host, is done by a one-request, one-reply channel between the dsh tool command and the host's tool endpoint, on the harness's own newline-delimited JSON-RPC codec, keeping every defensive rule upstream wraps around the library (bounded messages, a method allow-list, a pending call failed once on close, no transport timeouts, a revision check).

Upstream source imports esbuild once, for a type in the hot-reload error handler; otherwise it is a dependency of the script runner, the front-end bundler and the test runner, and it never runs in a packaged product. Go source is compiled ahead of time by the Go toolchain, so nothing is transpiled or bundled.

The entry lets esbuild's npm install script run so that it can select its prebuilt native program. Go has no install scripts: go mod download fetches source and executes nothing, and every dependency is compiled from source, so there is nothing to allow.

title: Tools from scripts (replaces the PTC guest runtime): own dsh tool command and host endpoint behind the guarded tool pipeline; no embedded interpreter and no JavaScript engine (owner decision OD-2)
No embedded interpreter: scripts call tools through the dsh tool command (owner decision OD-2, 2026-11-18)
A script is an ordinary sandboxed command, and the tool command finds the host through that command's environment
A call token carries exactly the calling agent's right to propose tool calls; every sub-call is checked and logged like a native call
The harness neither parses nor rewrites script text; there is no program form and no interpreter state
The script-calling prompt contract is generated by the harness and checked by a golden file
Each outcome of the tool command is one tabled exit code and error kind, and nothing is replayed after a restart
Tool names are plain strings looked up among the agent's tools, and a failed tool is a distinct exit code that names the tool
Sub-calls pass policy, guards and approval, follow native scheduling, and are logged as start and settle pairs before the outer result
The sub-call allowance refuses with the bound's name; the outer deadline cancels calls in flight, revokes the token and leaves no process
A harness-started command gets exactly the endpoint and token variables; without them the tool command is unavailable and contacts nothing
A token cannot reach another agent's tools or another session, a forged or expired token is refused, and the token value is masked
Standard output is exactly one JSON document; hostile traffic on the tool endpoint fails one connection and never the host
Malformed arguments are refused with a position before anything is sent, and script text is logged unchanged
Usage text, prompt section, tool list and schemas match a golden file and are absent when script calling is off
Subagent and external-provider tools are called through the same command and pipeline; a not-callable tool is refused and nesting stops at one level
JavaScript parser and tree walker used to rewrite guest programs: no parser and no engine in the Go harness
Script text reaches its interpreter unchanged, and no JavaScript parser or engine is linked into the binary
JavaScript scope analysis for the ES-module-to-CommonJS transform: nothing to rewrite in Go
Regular-expression parsing for exported schema patterns: regexp and regexp/syntax
Invalid patterns fail schema derivation by type and field; non-portable patterns are refused
Source excerpt with a caret for positioned errors: one own plain-text function
Excerpt shows the line, a caret at the column and the message, with no escape characters
Call channel between the dsh tool command and the host's tool endpoint: the harness NDJSON JSON-RPC codec
One request and one reply per connection with a hostile peer: bounds, allow-list, close and revision check
TypeScript and JavaScript compiler used by development tooling: replaced by the Go toolchain
The release build succeeds offline from the module cache with cgo off, and the binary runs with no source tree
Worker threads: goroutines with context for background work, child processes where a hard stop or isolation is needed
Background jobs are bounded, cancelled when their fiber unloads, and leak no goroutine
A helper process that ignores its stop request is killed within the grace period and has an explicit environment
Module-loader interface: embedded assets, explicit program lookup and build-time version
Embedded assets are served from an empty directory, a missing external program is named, and one version is reported everywhere
V8 inspector session: Go profiler and execution tracer behind owner-only loopback endpoints
Profiling routes are off by default and, when enabled, loopback-only and owner-only
